passage:
"So? How was week six?" Lokesh asked, reaching for the papad.
"Actually good," Meenal said. "Ritesh sir and I have a Monday check-in now. Fifteen minutes. And he wrote down what a finished report should look like. One page."
"The same Ritesh who embarrassed you in front of everyone?" Appa put down his spoon.
"Same one. After I asked to talk privately, things changed. He even said my question list was useful."
"You went and told your boss how to give feedback?" Lokesh grinned. "Brave."
"I didn't tell him. I asked. Politely."
Her father, Shankar, nodded slowly. "When I was young, I would have just stayed angry for a year."
"I almost did, Appa. It was worse."

qa.q: How long is Meenal's Monday check-in?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What does Meenal's 'I almost did, Appa. It was worse' suggest she has learned?
qa.a: She seems to feel that swallowing her anger was more painful than speaking up, and she's relieved she chose to raise it.

qa.q: Which working habits helped Meenal and Ritesh sir move forward?
qa.a: A short weekly check-in and a written description of a finished report, which replaced guessing with clear expectations.

qa.q: How does Shankar seem to see his daughter's approach?
qa.a: He seems impressed and a little reflective, comparing it with how he would have stayed angry for a year when he was young.

grounding: At dinner a young woman tells her family how a weekly check-in and written expectations followed her respectful complaint, building trust with her senior.

passage: Three months into my internship, I, Leela, finally understand what happened with Chetan. For weeks I'd been the quiet new girl, sitting on my resentment: the public corrections, the one-word emails. After we talked privately, we tried something simple. Every Friday at four, ten minutes at his desk. And a shared document titled 'What done looks like', where he wrote the standard for every task before I started it. The first Friday felt stiff. By the fourth, I was bringing my own list of questions, and he was asking what I thought. Last week he disagreed with my plan, and I said, 'I see it differently,' out loud, in a meeting. He said, 'Good point, let's try yours.' Swallowing it never got me that. Saying it respectfully did.

qa.q: What was the shared document titled?
qa.a: It was titled 'What done looks like'.

qa.q: How did Leela feel during the first Friday check-in compared with the fourth?
qa.a: The first felt stiff and awkward, but by the fourth she felt confident enough to bring her own questions, suggesting growing trust.

qa.q: Why did the weekly check-in and shared document help?
qa.a: They made expectations clear before work began and gave a regular, safe place to raise problems, so resentment didn't build up.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Leela now compared with before?
qa.a: He probably sees her as a contributor whose views are worth hearing, since he now asks her opinion and accepted her plan.

grounding: A young woman looks back on how a weekly check-in and written standards turned swallowed resentment into respectful disagreement and trust.

passage:
Supervisor's note, end of month two
Hafsa and I now meet every Monday at 9:30 for fifteen minutes. We keep a shared document listing what "done" looks like for each task: format, sources, deadline. This came out of a hard talk three weeks ago, after I corrected her in a meeting and she asked, very calmly, to discuss it privately.
Since then, I've seen a change. She raises small problems early, like last week, when she told me a data file was incomplete before it became a crisis. Today she disagreed with one of my suggestions and explained why, and she was right. I told her so.
Next step: I'll ask her to draft the checklist for the next intern.
Hansa, research lead

qa.q: When do Hafsa and Hansa meet every week?
qa.a: Every Monday at 9:30, for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What does Hafsa disagreeing with a suggestion suggest about how she now feels?
qa.a: She seems more confident and trusting, feeling safe enough to raise problems and disagree respectfully.

qa.q: Why is asking Hafsa to draft the next intern's checklist a good next step?
qa.a: It shows trust in her growth and passes on the written expectations that helped her.

qa.q: How has Hansa's view of Hafsa changed since the hard talk?
qa.a: Hansa now sees Hafsa as someone who flags issues early and thinks independently, and says so openly.

grounding: Shows a supervisor's note on agreeing weekly check-ins and written expectations, and the trust that grew after conflict was raised respectfully.

passage:
Diary, Friday
Third weekly check-in with Lalremsiami today. Fifteen minutes, her office, Friday at four. We go through the list we wrote together: what's due, what "good" means for each thing, and anything bothering either of us.
Today I told her the Thursday deadlines are too tight when data comes Wednesday night. I said it calmly and she moved them to Friday. Just like that!
A month ago I'd have swallowed it and complained to the other interns. I was that girl who smiled in meetings and cried in the washroom. Now I say things. Weirdly, she trusts me more because of it. She even asked me what I'd change about the internship.
Rehana

qa.q: When is Rehana's weekly check-in with Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Friday at four, for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How was Rehana feeling when the deadline was moved?
qa.a: She felt surprised and pleased, even proud, that raising it calmly worked.

qa.q: Which habit is helping Rehana most at this stage?
qa.a: Using the weekly check-in and written list to raise issues calmly, instead of swallowing them.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami seem to see Rehana now?
qa.a: She seems to trust Rehana more and values her opinion, even asking what she would change.

grounding: Shows an intern's diary about weekly check-ins and written expectations, and learning that raising issues respectfully builds trust.

passage:
Binita: Hi Rukmini, reminder: check-in tomorrow at 10. I've updated our expectations doc 📋
Rukmini: Thanks! I read it. Can I add one thing?
Binita: Of course
Rukmini: For drafts, could you mark which comments are must-fix and which are suggestions? I lose time guessing
Binita: Great point. Adding it now
Rukmini: Also, honestly, I'm glad we started these. Last month I was so angry after that meeting I nearly quit
Binita: I know. I'm glad you told me instead of quitting. It made me a better lead
Rukmini: 🙂
Binita: See you at 10. Bring your list

qa.q: What did Rukmini ask Binita to mark on drafts?
qa.a: Which comments are must-fix and which are suggestions.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling on admitting to nearly quitting?
qa.a: Rukmini felt relieved and grateful, glad the check-ins replaced last month's anger.

qa.q: Why does adding Rukmini's point to the doc help?
qa.a: It turns a frustration into a clear, written agreement, so conflict gets solved instead of swallowed.

qa.q: How does Binita see Rukmini's honesty?
qa.a: Binita values it and says it made for a better lead, showing trust has grown on both sides.

grounding: Shows an intern and senior using weekly check-ins and written expectations, with the intern learning that raising issues builds trust.

passage: Every Monday at nine, before farmers started queuing at the cooperative counter in the kasba, Yamini and Pallavi now sat for fifteen minutes with two cups of tea and a notebook. Yamini had written the week's expectations in plain Marathi and English: which ledgers to update, which receipts needed her signature, when to ask. Pallavi kept her own column headed "questions". A month ago she would have spent the week guessing, then sulked when Yamini frowned at her work. After the tense morning over the torn ledger page, she had finally said so, politely, and Yamini had listened. Today Pallavi raised a small complaint: the milk-collection slips kept reaching her late. Yamini nodded, wrote it down and called the clerk. Pallavi walked back to her desk lighter, surprised at how much easier the office felt.

qa.q: When do Yamini and Pallavi meet each week?
qa.a: Every Monday at nine, for fifteen minutes, before farmers start queuing at the counter.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi walk back to her desk lighter?
qa.a: She felt relieved and more trusted, because she raised a complaint and Yamini took it seriously instead of brushing it off.

qa.q: What makes this Monday habit work?
qa.a: Written expectations remove the guessing, and the questions column gives Pallavi a set place to raise problems early and politely.

qa.q: How might this routine help Yamini?
qa.a: Yamini hears about problems like the late slips early, so she can fix them before they turn into frowns and tension.

grounding: Shows a weekly check-in and written expectations after a conflict, and a young worker finding that raising issues respectfully builds trust.
